performers: Royal Choral Society; Royal Albert Hall Orchestra; Malcolm Sargent, conductor
question: How do longer phrases change the relation between declaration and counterpoint?
intro: Sargent conducts the Royal Choral Society and Royal Albert Hall Orchestra in a recording made at the Albert Hall on 2 April 1926. Its Electrola issue preserves a longer account of the chorus than the site’s Scherchen recording; compare phrase lengths rather than assuming the transferred sound reproduces the hall’s original balance.

sections.label: Opening span
sections.mNote: measured listening spans, not word-aligned choral entries

cues.title: A concert preserved on disc
cues.text: Follow the choir’s phrase endings as well as its attacks. This performance was recorded during a Royal Albert Hall concert: the disc preserves its timing, but the surviving balance is not a transparent reproduction of every listener’s position in the hall.
cues.evidence: The German National Library catalogue identifies the recording as made during the 2 April 1926 concert at the Royal Albert Hall. The comparison of phrase endings is a general listening suggestion. https://d-nb.info/380148439

cues.title: The named performing forces
cues.text: The source names the Royal Choral Society, Royal Albert Hall Orchestra and Malcolm Sargent. It gives no singer count: the apparent mass of the transferred sound cannot by itself establish how many people performed.
cues.evidence: The Public Domain Project supplies all three credits; the library catalogue independently identifies the choir and orchestra. Neither consulted record gives a headcount. http://pool.publicdomainproject.org/index.php?title=Electrola-ej39-04871

cues.title: A marked withdrawal
cues.text: The sound falls back substantially before recovering. Compare the length of this quieter stretch with the surrounding stronger phrases, without using the transfer’s level as a measure of the choir’s absolute loudness.
cues.evidence: The analysis shows a boundary at 1:28, relative levels around −25 dB at 1:30–1:35 and renewed level around 1:40. These are within-recording measurements, not matched score bars.

cues.title: The side has an identity
cues.text: The transferred side is Electrola EJ 39, label number 04871, matrix E-CR.237-1A. Such identifiers distinguish a specific issued record from the broader fact that Sargent performed Messiah many times.
cues.evidence: The German National Library identifies EJ 39 side 2 of 2, matrix E-CR.237-1A and label number 04871. https://d-nb.info/380148439

cues.title: Continuity through changing sound
cues.text: In the central stretch, follow how each line continues while the combined sound changes. Compare phrase lengths with Scherchen’s recording rather than assuming that a longer total duration means uniformly broader singing.
cues.evidence: The analysis finds several feature boundaries between 2:32 and 2:58. They locate a changing region, not individual voice entries; the separate provisional map compares its timing with Scherchen.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: One year remains disputed
cues.text: Commons gives the first release as 1927; the current upstream catalogue says 1926. Both are early enough for the stated European recording-rights expiry, but neither establishes that the sound recording is public domain in the United States.
cues.evidence: The two source records disagree on first issue, while agreeing on the 2 April 1926 session. The dossier retains the discrepancy and uses a territorial recording-rights basis, not the composition-only PD-old-70 tag. http://pool.publicdomainproject.org/index.php?title=Electrola-ej39-04871

cues.title: Closing sound and surface noise
cues.text: Attend to the spacing of the last gestures, then distinguish their release from the noise remaining on the transferred side. The final spike in a digital level trace need not be an orchestral accent.
cues.evidence: The report shows a quieter window around 4:00, stronger windows at 4:05–4:10 and a fall by 4:15, followed by irregular terminal energy. Alignment ends at 258 seconds rather than incorporating the last transfer tail.

composer.epithet: A German-trained composer of Italian opera who made the English chorus an actor in public musical drama.
facts: With Friedrich Wilhelm Zachow in Halle; theatre work in Hamburg; study and commissions in Italy, 1706–10
Hanover briefly; settled in London in 1712; became a British subject in 1727
Italian operas, English oratorios, anthems, concertos, chamber cantatas and ceremonial orchestral music
composer.background:
Handel grew up in Halle, the son of a barber-surgeon, and studied with Friedrich Wilhelm Zachow, organist of the town’s principal church. Zachow’s teaching included counterpoint, keyboard playing and the copying of other composers’ music. Handel briefly enrolled at the university and held an organist’s post before moving to Hamburg in 1703. Its public opera house offered a different education: he played in the orchestra and encountered the practical demands of singers, stage machinery and mixed theatrical repertory. His first opera, Almira, was performed there in 1705, with a German text incorporating Italian arias.

From 1706 to 1710 Handel worked in Italy, writing cantatas, sacred music and opera for patrons in Florence, Rome, Naples and Venice. Rome gave him access to virtuoso singers and to instrumentalists associated with Corelli. The Latin Dixit Dominus of 1707 demands rapid, independent choral lines and sustained control of dissonance; the chamber cantatas make emotional turns within much smaller forces. Agrippina, performed in Venice at the end of 1709, assembles much previously written material into a calculated theatrical comedy. Reuse was already part of his method: a successful musical gesture could acquire a different function when assigned to a new character and situation.
